description: A credential that outlives the thing it admits, read from one call that says both what to write when a record is new and what to write when it already exists. The insert half is this program's own statement of what a new record of that kind needs, so the absence in the update half is decided against the program's own convention rather than against a population -- which is what makes an absence rule sayable here at all. The positive mints a signing token on insert and rewrites the recipient's address on update, leaving the link mailed to the old address admitting its holder to the new one; it is documenso's `set-document-recipients.ts:155` written out, and the same sentence as healthchecks' fixed email-verification token. Three negatives, one for each fact the rule requires. The near miss rewrites the address AND reissues the token, which is the fix and is otherwise the identical call. The second update rewrites a sort order and a send status, which the token is not about -- rotating a credential because a row moved would be a nuisance rather than a repair. The third is an ordinary create with no existing-record half, where nothing failed to rotate because the row did not exist. Measured over ten production repositories this shape matches twice and both are the weakness; the broader shape it was reshaped from -- a create somewhere in the program naming a credential and an update elsewhere not naming it -- matches 173 times.

expected.note: the create half mints `token` and the update half rewrites `email` without it, so the credential no longer covers the address it was issued for
